title: Winner Detection
unlocks: Your game. In a browser. Playing your C++.
objective: Detect a win on any of the eight lines and a draw on a full board. Then implement ttt::Game so the course's web server can run the game you built.
creates: win detection in your existing files

cpp: inheriting from an interface (used now, explained at Stage 7)
linux: reaching a WSL2 port from Windows

checks: All eight winning lines are detected, for both players.
A full board with no line is a draw, not a win.
A snapshot you took earlier does not change when you play a move.
Two calls to createGame() give two independent games.
hints: How many distinct sets of three cells win the game? Write them all down on paper before you write any code. Getting the count right is most of this stage.

There are two separate questions here, and mixing them is what makes this hard: (a) which triples of positions are winning lines, and (b) do these three cells hold the same non-empty mark? Write them as two different things.

That table can be a `std::array<std::array<int, 3>, 8>` declared once, and a loop over it. If you find yourself typing the eighth `if` statement, stop and go back to hint 3.

For the adapter: put `ttt::createGame()` at the BOTTOM of Adapter.cpp, not in its own file. A factory function in a file you forgot to add to CMakeLists.txt produces a linker error that looks like a mystery.

prompts.title: My win detection misses cases
prompts.body:
My tic-tac-toe game does not always notice a win.

Here is my win-checking code:
<PASTE IT>

Here is a board where it goes wrong:
<DESCRIBE THE BOARD AND WHO SHOULD HAVE WON>

Ask me to trace through my own code by hand for that board before you say anything about the cause. Then ask which lines my code actually checks.

prompts.title: Review my win-detection approach
prompts.body:
I have written win detection for tic-tac-toe.

Here is my code:
<PASTE IT>

Ask me questions rather than rewriting it. Specifically: how many places would I have to change to support a 4x4 board, is my 'is this line a win' logic written once or eight times, and how would I test this without playing a whole game? Do not give me code.

prompts.title: Quiz me on Stage 5
prompts.body:
Quiz me on what I just built: iterating a table of winning lines, std::optional, and the idea of implementing an interface someone else defined.

One question at a time, wait for me. Include the interview-style question: 'why is a table of winning lines better than eight if statements, and what does it cost you?' Push back if my answer is vague.
